newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to hand over Bosnian arms as officials sacked.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to hand over Bosnian arms as officials sacked.

text.p: The United States will begin delivering a delayed arms shipment to Bosnia following the ousting of two defence officials in the country's Moslem-Croat federation, the State Department said on Wednesday.

Spokesman Glyn Davies said the ship American Condor, which has been at anchor in the Adriatic for several weeks, would now dock at the Croatian port of Ploce and begin offloading nearly $100 million worth of hardware destined for Bosnia.
He said this could happen as soon as Thursday.
Washington had been holding up the delivery, which includes tanks, helicopters and howitzers, to back its demand for the sacking of the Federation's Deputy Defence Minister, Hasan Cengic.

U.S. officials alleged that Cengic, a Moslem, had close ties with Iran and was likely to obstruct the U.S.-sponsored "Train and Equip" programme for the Federation's armed forces, of which the arms delivery is a key component.
Davies told reporters that Federation President Kresimir Zubak had agreed to replace Cengic as of Wednesday and also accepted the resignation of Defence Minister Vladimir Soljic.

"We now have in hand copies of the written orders making these changes from Zubak's office, and we have also received assurances from Bosnian President (Alija) Izetbegovic that Mr Cengic is no longer serving as deputy minister," he said.

The State Department has never detailed its objections to Soljic, a Croat. He resigned on Tuesday amid rumours that he would be forced to step down along with Cengic as part of a package deal which would be billed as a reorganisation.

The arms delivery will allow the controversial Train and Equip programme, aimed at making the Moslems and Croats a military match for the Serbs whom they fought in Bosnia's 43-month war, to finally get off the ground.
The programme is being managed by a private American contractor under supervision of U.S. official James Pardew.

In other Balkan developments, Davies denounced an attempt by the Croatian government to force an independent radio station off the air, and expressed concern at alleged manipulation of results in municipal elections in Serbia.

In Croatia, the popular Radio 101 said on Wednesday that the government-controlled Telecommunications Council had awarded its frequency to Radio Globus 101 which is being set up by a tycoon closely linked to the ruling HDZ party.
"This development ... constitutes in our view a significant setback for democratization and free expression in (Croatia)," Davies said.

"As Croatia pursues closer ties with the West, we believe it essential that the government of Croatia respect the rules of a democratic society", he said, in a hint that Washington might try to block Zagreb's bid to join Western groupings.

He said the issue would have a high priority on the U.S. agenda with Croatia. Washington would raise it with the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe and also propose that members of the Council of Europe discuss it.
In Serbia, Davies said the United States was "very concerned by the apparent failure of the Serbian authorities to observe democratic norms" in vote-counting after local elections last weekend.

Serbian opposition parties have accused the ruling Socialists of President Slobodan Milosevic of massive fraud in trying to cancel results in areas where the opposition was initially said to have won.
"We call on Serbian authorities to ensure that procedural manoeuvres are not used to annul the legitimate votes of the Serbian people," Davies said.
